1 Introduction

Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have become critical to a widening range of visual tasks such as image generation and curation (Liu et al., 2023, Team et al., 2023, Wang et al., 2024). Many of these applications require aesthetic judgment, asking models to compare visual works and identify differences in execution quality across composition, color harmony, technical execution, and cultural convention. This makes aesthetic judgment a demanding test of higher-order multimodal reasoning that is often omitted by existing visual benchmarks (Yu et al., 2023, Yue et al., 2024).

Existing image-aesthetics datasets and methods typically reduce aesthetic judgment to a mapping from an image to a scalar score (Murray et al., 2012, Kong et al., 2016, He et al., 2022, Lee and Kim, 2019, Hosu et al., 2019, Yi et al., 2023, He et al., 2023), an approach that we argue is poorly suited to the underlying decision being studied. Preference order is inferred from independent scores rather than measured through direct comparison; crowd-averaged labels mix expertise, taste, and annotation noise, so the aesthetic signal is difficult to isolate; and because images in such datasets often depict different subjects, a model can shortcut its way to high accuracy by exploiting content preferences instead of discriminating execution quality.

We first ask whether scoring faithfully captures comparative preference . Eight expert annotators evaluate the same images under both independent absolute scoring and direct comparative ranking, and the two protocols disagree. Comparative ranking yields 42 percentage points higher inter-annotator agreement on best-image selection than score-derived rankings (Talebi and Milanfar, 2018, Ma et al., 2017, Wu et al., 2023, Zhou et al., 2024a). The two protocols therefore elicit different preference signals from the same annotators, and direct comparison captures the underlying judgment more faithfully than the pointwise scoring used in most existing pipelines.

Building on this finding, we introduce the Visual Aesthetic Benchmark (VAB), which formulates aesthetic judgment as a comparative selection problem over candidate sets with matched subject matter. VAB contains 400 tasks and 1,195 images across fine art, photography, and illustration, covering 24 topics (Figure 1). Each task presents two to six images sharing a common subject, and the model selects the best image and, under the stricter setting, also the worst image. Three design choices distinguish VAB from prior aesthetic benchmarks. Matched subject matter within each task isolates differences in execution from differences in content; each ground-truth label is the consensus of 10 independent expert judges, filtered through a dual-threshold criterion to remove ambiguous cases; and every task is evaluated under three independent random permutations of the candidate order. We report ap@1, the average accuracy across the three evaluations, and pass^3, which credits a task only when the model is correct in all three.

We benchmark 20 frontier MLLMs and six dedicated visual-quality reward models on VAB. The strongest system, Claude Sonnet 4.6, reaches 26.5% on TB-1 pass^3, 42.4 points below the human baseline of 68.9%. Models are also highly sensitive to candidate order, retaining only 34–65% of their ap@1 accuracy when required to be correct across all three permutations, and they degrade much faster than humans as the candidate set grows: a ⟦SLOT_0⟧ drop from two-image to four-or-more-image tasks, against only ⟦SLOT_1⟧ for human experts. The contributions of this paper are as follows.

• A controlled human study with eight expert annotators establishes that direct comparative ranking is substantially more reliable than independent scoring for subjective aesthetic annotation, and motivates the design of the benchmark.

• VAB is, to our knowledge, the first set-based, expert-grounded, multi-domain aesthetic benchmark with permutation-robust evaluation, covering 400 tasks and 1,195 images across fine art, photography, and illustration.

• A systematic evaluation of 20 frontier MLLMs and six dedicated reward models exposes a persistent 42.4-point gap to human experts on TB-1 pass^3 together with severe positional instability across permutations of the candidate order.

• Fine-tuning on 2,000 expert examples brings a 35B-parameter model close to a 397B-parameter open-weight model, indicating that expert comparative judgments transfer effectively through lightweight adaptation.
2 Human Annotation Study: Ranking vs. Scoring

Existing aesthetic benchmarks rely on Scoring to collect ground truth labels (Murray et al., 2012, Kong et al., 2016, He et al., 2022, Cao et al., 2025). We conduct a controlled human study to explore the following research question regarding the annotation process:
Which protocol yields a more scientifically sound signal for data annotation?
• Scoring: expert annotates each image independently on an absolute aesthetic scale.
• Ranking: expert compares images and annotates their relative order.
Setup and Metrics.

Eight expert annotators evaluate the same images under two protocols: (1) scoring assigns each image an independent score ⟦SLOT_2⟧; (2) ranking orders images directly within groups of size ⟦SLOT_3⟧. We construct 119 homogeneous-content tasks, in which all candidates share the same underlying content, and 107 heterogeneous-content tasks formed by regrouping images across source groups while preserving topic consistency. We compare the two protocols along three dimensions:

• Fidelity (Kendall’s ⟦SLOT_4⟧ (Kendall, 1938)): we compute ⟦SLOT_5⟧, where ⟦SLOT_6⟧ and ⟦SLOT_7⟧ are the numbers of concordant and discordant pairs between an annotator’s score-derived ranking ⟦SLOT_8⟧ and the same annotator’s direct comparison. A low ⟦SLOT_9⟧ means the two protocols elicit different preference orderings from the same person. We additionally report the top-1 self-consistency (SC) rate: the fraction of annotator–task pairs for which ⟦SLOT_10⟧ and the direct comparison select the same top image.

• Reproducibility (⟦SLOT_11⟧): ⟦SLOT_12⟧ is the proportion of tasks where a single image receives ⟦SLOT_13⟧ of 8 best-image votes; ⟦SLOT_14⟧ and ⟦SLOT_15⟧ are defined analogously. Higher accuracy means the protocol produces ground truth labels that different experts can independently reproduce.

• Distinguishability (top-1 entropy (Shannon, 1948)): we measure ⟦SLOT_16⟧, where ⟦SLOT_17⟧ is the fraction of annotators selecting image ⟦SLOT_18⟧ as best. Lower entropy means annotators concentrate on a single top choice rather than spreading votes.
Full protocol details, notations, formal definitions, and statistical tests are in Appendix F.
Scoring does not faithfully preserve preference order.

Table 1 shows that score-derived rankings often diverge from the direct comparisons given by the same annotator. The mean Kendall’s ⟦SLOT_19⟧ is 0.188 for homogeneous-content and 0.351 for heterogeneous-content tasks; the top-1 self-consistency rates are 45.5% and 52.0%, respectively. In other words, nearly half of the numeric score annotations fail to recover the order that the same annotator expresses under direct comparison.

Ranking yields more reproducible labels.

Table 2 shows that ranking yields substantially higher inter-annotator agreement on best and worst labels. On homogeneous-content tasks, ranking improves ⟦SLOT_24⟧ by 42.0 points, ⟦SLOT_25⟧ by 37.0 points, and ⟦SLOT_26⟧ by 51.3 points (all ⟦SLOT_27⟧, McNemar test (McNemar, 1947)); the same pattern holds for heterogeneous-content tasks. Independent experts can therefore reproduce best/worst labels far more reliably under ranking than under scoring.

Ranking makes the top choice stand out more clearly.

Table 3 measures how concentrated their top-choice preference is within each task. It shows that ranking produces lower entropy over top-1 selections (Shannon, 1948) (0.729 vs. 1.213) and a much higher rate of unanimous choices (10.1% vs. 0.8%; Wilcoxon ⟦SLOT_55⟧ (Wilcoxon, 1945)). More generally, ranking concentrates votes on a single preferred image rather than spreading them across several plausible winners.

Interpretation.

Our findings align with conclusions from two complementary disciplines. Aesthetically, modern aesthetics favors a relational view of beauty (Goldman, 1995, Levinson, 2005): people judge preference more reliably when alternatives are juxtaposed than when items are assessed in isolation. Cognitively, comparative judgment is a more primitive operation than absolute evaluation (Thurstone, 1927). Absolute scoring requires maintaining an internal reference scale and converting qualitative impressions into numbers, imposing heavier cognitive load and greater instability (Stewart et al., 2005, Parducci, 1965).
We therefore adopt ranking as the annotation protocol for VAB. Extended discussion is provided in Appendix F.2.
3 The VAB Benchmark

Building on the findings of Section 2, we construct the Visual Aesthetic Benchmark (VAB) to test whether frontier multimodal models can make expert-aligned aesthetic judgments under a ranking-based protocol. In contrast with prior evaluations that aggregate scalar ratings from crowd annotators (Murray et al., 2012, Kong et al., 2016, He et al., 2022), VAB casts aesthetic evaluation as comparative selection over candidate sets with matched subject matter: each task asks the model to identify the best image and, in the stricter setting, also the worst. The remainder of this section describes the task layout, the data construction pipeline, and the ground-truth formation procedure.
3.1 Overview
Figure 2: Detailed distribution of VAB.

Task formulation. Each benchmark task presents a candidate set of images with matched subject matter, so performance depends on differences in execution rather than differences in depicted content. VAB contains 400 released tasks and 1,195 images across fine art, photography, and illustration, covering 24 topics with candidate set sizes from 2 to 6 images. We consider two settings: in Top-1, the model selects the best image in the set; in TB-1, it identifies both the best and the worst image. Figure 1 provides a visual overview, Figure 2 summarizes the released domain and topic distribution, and Appendix B.1 reports detailed benchmark statistics.

Evaluation protocol. Labels are derived from direct comparative judgments by independent experts rather than post hoc aggregation of absolute scores. Each task is evaluated three times, each under an independent random permutation of the candidate order. We report ap@1, the average accuracy across the three evaluations, and pass^3, which counts a task as correct only if the model is correct in all three. Representative topic-level examples are collected in Appendix I.
3.2 Data Construction

Figure 3: Overview of the VAB data construction pipeline. Images are organized into candidate sets with matched subject matter and varying aesthetic execution, then passed through expert review and consensus filtering before entering the benchmark.

Because VAB is annotated through direct ranking over candidate sets, data construction is organized around matched image groups rather than standalone images: in every domain, the members of a set share subject matter but vary in execution quality. Figure 3 summarizes the pipeline; Appendix B.2 reports the full raw-pool statistics, and Appendix B.3 contains the domain-level construction details.

Fine Art. We commissioned 426 painting sets comprising 1,142 images. Each set is built from constrained artist prompts that preserve subject matter while allowing variation in composition, value structure, color handling, and finish. All works were commissioned specifically for VAB.

Photography. We constructed 670 photography sets comprising 1,809 images. Each set originates from a single source photograph, many provided directly by professional photographers, and is expanded through two pipelines: an expert-edit pipeline based on professional retouching tools, which can produce either original/improved pairs or larger multi-expert sets, and a scalable agent-edit pipeline that generates improved and degraded variants. The agent-edit prompt sequence and runtime pipeline are recorded in Appendix H.1.

Illustration. We constructed 271 illustration sets comprising 908 images. These sets are formed either by prompt-based generation with text-to-image models or by rendering CC0 3D assets under controlled viewpoint and presentation changes, producing multiple images with matched subject matter but varying execution. Prompt templates are in Appendix H.2.
All collected sets are deduplicated and reviewed for semantic consistency before annotation.
3.3 Expert Annotation and Ground Truth
Following Section 2, VAB uses ranking-based expert consensus for ground truth.

Review setup. Creation and evaluation are strictly separated. In the raw pre-filter pool, each collected candidate set is reviewed by 10 independent expert judges drawn from a pool of more than 100 evaluators, yielding over 13,000 assessments and more than 300 hours of review. Judges remain blind to artist identity throughout annotation. Rubrics and interface examples are in Appendix C. Additional topic-level examples are in Appendix I.

Annotation protocol. Each task presents ⟦SLOT_60⟧ candidate images side by side. Judges first assess each image against the domain-specific rubric and then make a comparative selection over the full set. For ⟦SLOT_61⟧, a judge selects the best image. For ⟦SLOT_62⟧, a judge selects both the best and the worst image, with distinct choices required. Every task receives exactly 10 judgments. A representative annotation example is shown in Figure 4.

Figure 4: Example of a single VAB annotation task, illustrating the candidate set presented to expert judges and the resulting consensus decision. The consensus threshold is determined through statistical confidence; see Appendix D for details.

Consensus filter. A task is retained only if expert votes are sufficiently concentrated. For ⟦SLOT_63⟧, the best-image votes must meet the threshold; for ⟦SLOT_64⟧, the best-image and worst-image votes must both meet it, so satisfying only one is insufficient. The thresholds are chosen by statistical confidence under a uniform-random null, and the exact derivation and threshold table are provided in Appendix D.
4 Experiments
4.1 Setup
Evaluation scope. We evaluate 20 MLLMs and six reward models on VAB. Unless otherwise noted, each model is evaluated under its default inference configuration.

We compare all systems against two baselines. The Human Expert baseline is obtained from a fresh round of annotation in which 10 expert judges evaluate each released task under the benchmark interface, and we report their average accuracy against the released labels. The Random Guess baseline is computed analytically for each task size ⟦SLOT_65⟧.
MLLMs.

Our MLLM evaluation covers 20 closed-source and open-weight models spanning the Claude family (Anthropic, 2026a, Anthropic, 2025a, Anthropic, 2026b, Anthropic, 2025b, Anthropic, 2026c), the Gemini family (Google DeepMind, 2025a, Google DeepMind, 2025c, Google DeepMind, 2026), GPT and o-series models (OpenAI, 2025a, OpenAI, 2025e, OpenAI, 2025c, OpenAI, 2025b, OpenAI, 2025d, OpenAI, 2025f), and additional systems from Doubao, Grok, GLM, Kimi, and Qwen (ByteDance Seed, 2026, xAI, 2025, Z.ai, 2025, Team et al., 2026, Bai et al., 2023, Qwen Team, 2026). For each task, the model selects either the best image (Top-1) or both the best and worst images (TB-1). We evaluate each task three times under independent random permutations of candidate order and report ap@1 and pass^3 as defined in Section 3. Prompts are provided in Appendix H.3.
Reward Models.

We additionally evaluate six reward models: ArtiMuse (Cao et al., 2025), PEAS-aes and PEAS-ava (Yun and Choo, 2024), Q-Align (Wu et al., 2023), Q-Instruct (Wu et al., 2024), and RealQA-ava (Li et al., 2025). Unlike MLLMs, these models assign scalar scores to images independently rather than selecting directly from a set. We therefore follow each model’s official scoring interface, score each image three times, average the scores, and then rank images within each task. The main text reports Top-1 and TB-1; model-specific scoring interfaces and full result tables, including Bot-1 and topic-level breakdowns, are deferred to Appendix H.4, Appendix E.2, and Appendix E.4.

Gap to experts. Current frontier models remain far below expert performance. On the strictest metric, TB-1 pass^3, Claude Sonnet 4.6 attains 26.5%, against 68.9% for human experts; even under the more lenient TB-1 ap@1, the strongest model, Doubao Seed 2.0 Pro, reaches 42.8%, still 26.1 points short of the expert baseline.

Progress across families. Improvements are uneven across model families. Claude Sonnet 4.6 nearly doubles its predecessor on TB-1 pass^3 (14.5% ⟦SLOT_66⟧ 26.5%), whereas the GPT-5 series regresses from 21.8% (GPT-5) to 20.0% (GPT-5.1) and 15.5% (GPT-5.2). A clear closed/open gap persists under the stricter metric: the strongest open-weight system, Qwen3.5-397B-A17B, reaches 17.2% on TB-1 pass^3, compared with 26.5% for Claude Sonnet 4.6.

Domain difficulty and stability. Accuracy varies strongly across domains and across repeated evaluations. Illustration is the most difficult domain, where Claude Sonnet 4.6 attains only 19.0% on TB-1 pass^3, while photography is comparatively more tractable, with o4-mini reaching 30.2%. The large ap@1-to-pass^3 gap—for example, GLM-4.6V drops from 34.1% to 11.5% on TB-1—indicates that sensitivity to candidate order and response instability remain major failure modes.

Overall performance. Reward models also remain well below human experts, although some are competitive with MLLMs on Top-1. Q-Align is the strongest overall, reaching 52.2% on Top-1 and 38.2% on TB-1, against 77.7% and 68.9% for the human baseline.

Domain trends and asymmetric failure modes. Domain trends broadly mirror the MLLM results. Appendix E.2 additionally reveals an asymmetry between best and worst predictions: Q-Instruct reaches 51.5% on overall Bot-1 and 77.0% on photography Bot-1, despite considerably weaker Top-1 scores of 38.5% overall and 43.9% in photography. This pattern suggests that detecting aesthetic failure is in some cases easier than identifying the strongest image in a set.

Comparison with MLLMs. The best reward-model Top-1 result , 52.2%, is numerically close to the best MLLM Top-1 ap@1 result , 55.4%, but the comparison is not strictly like-for-like: MLLMs make a single comparative decision over a candidate set, whereas reward models score images independently and are then ranked within the set.
4.3 Ablations and Additional Analysis

Temperature ablation. For models with an exposed temperature parameter, greedy decoding improves Top-1 pass^3 by 1.1 points on average and TB-1 pass^3 by 2.3 points. Decoding stochasticity therefore contributes noise, but it does not explain the main performance gap; full model-by-model results are reported in Appendix E.5.

Candidate set size. Performance degrades sharply as the candidate set grows. Under TB-1 pass^3, the best model falls from 47.3% on two-image tasks to 6.7% on four-image tasks, while human experts decline from 87.1% to 43.6%. Larger candidate sets therefore amplify both comparative difficulty and instability; the full breakdown is reported in Appendix E.6.
5 Fine-Tuning on Expert Aesthetic Judgments
Training Setup.

We fine-tune Qwen3.5-35B-A3B using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) (Hu et al., 2022) with rank 64 and ⟦SLOT_67⟧, freezing the vision tower while updating the multimodal projector. Supervision comes from 2,000 additional expert-annotated examples collected with the same annotation pipeline described in Section 3.3; these examples are fully disjoint from the benchmark evaluation set. We train for three epochs with a learning rate of ⟦SLOT_68⟧ and cosine scheduling. Additional hyperparameters and full fine-tuning results are provided in Appendix G. The fine-tuned model is denoted as Kallisti-35B-A3B.

Improvement over the base model.

Table 6 compares Kallisti-35B-A3B against its base model and a set of open-weight baselines. Fine-tuning yields consistent gains across all four reported metrics: Top-1 pass^3 improves from 25.5% to 29.5%, TB-1 pass^3 from 15.8% to 17.5%, Top-1 ap@1 from 47.5% to 51.3%, and TB-1 ap@1 from 36.5% to 38.8%. The topic-level breakdown is reported in Appendix G.2.
Scaling implication.

Kallisti-35B-A3B approaches the substantially larger Qwen3.5-397B-A17B on Top-1 pass^3, 29.5% versus 29.8%, and lies within roughly one point on the other metrics. This is preliminary evidence that the comparative supervision in VAB carries enough aesthetic signal to compensate for an order-of-magnitude reduction in parameter count under lightweight adaptation.
6 Conclusion

We introduced VAB, a benchmark that recasts aesthetic evaluation as comparative selection over candidate sets with matched subject matter, with labels grounded in expert ranking rather than scalar scoring. VAB contains 400 tasks and 1,195 images spanning fine art, photography, and illustration. A controlled human study motivates the protocol: direct ranking yields 42 percentage points higher inter-annotator agreement than score-derived rankings. Across 20 frontier MLLMs and six reward models, the strongest system reaches 26.5% on TB-1 pass^3 against 68.9% for human experts, and accuracy drops sharply as the candidate set grows; models also exhibit pronounced positional instability across permutations of the candidate order. Fine-tuning a 35B-parameter model on 2,000 expert examples brings its accuracy close to that of a 397B-parameter open-weight model, suggesting that expert comparative supervision transfers efficiently with lightweight adaptation. We see several directions for future work: broadening domain and annotator diversity beyond the present three domains, improving robustness to candidate-order permutations, and scaling expert comparative supervision to larger training corpora. By making expert aesthetic judgment a measurable, comparative target, VAB establishes the foundation on which expert-aligned multimodal aesthetic judgment can now be systematically pursued.
Ethics Statement

This study involved human participants providing aesthetic judgments through an online evaluation platform. The University of Washington Human Subjects Division (HSD) reviewed the protocol and determined that the research qualifies as exempt human subjects research (Category 2 and 3; minimal-risk behavioral research) under U.S. federal regulations. Participation was voluntary and participants could stop at any time. No sensitive personal information was collected. Only aggregated benchmark results are publicly released, and no identifiable participant data are included in any publications or datasets. The exempt determination letter is on file with the authors.

All fine art works were created as commissioned works for VAB, with participating artists informed of and consenting to the use of their work for research. Professional photographers whose images served as source material for the photography pipeline contributed their work under appropriate licensing terms. Agent-edited variants derived from these source photographs were produced within the scope of those agreements. Illustration sets generated through text-to-image models used structured prompts without reproducing copyrighted material, and 3D-rendered sets were constructed exclusively from CC0-licensed assets. We are committed to crediting and fairly compensating all human creators whose work contributed to this benchmark.

Appendix A Related Work
Multimodal Large Language Models.

Recent MLLMs such as Flamingo, BLIP-2, InstructBLIP, LLaVA, Gemini, and Qwen2-VL have rapidly improved multimodal perception, instruction following, and reasoning (Alayrac et al., 2022, Li et al., 2023, Dai et al., 2023, Liu et al., 2023, Team et al., 2023, Wang et al., 2024). Their capabilities are typically assessed on broad benchmarks such as MM-Vet and MMMU (Yu et al., 2023, Yue et al., 2024), where each example usually admits a single correct answer. Aesthetic judgment is different: it is comparative, convention-sensitive, and not reducible to factual correctness alone. Our focus is therefore whether frontier MLLMs can make stable, expert-aligned selections over candidate sets with matched subject matter rather than pointwise judgments on isolated images.
Image Aesthetics Assessment.

Image aesthetics assessment (IAA) has traditionally been posed as single-image score prediction. Canonical datasets such as AVA and AADB provide large-scale photographic images with scalar ratings. Later resources extend this paradigm through comments, theme-aware labels, and personalization, including AVA-Reviews, TAD66K, and PARA (Murray et al., 2012, Kong et al., 2016, Wang et al., 2019, He et al., 2022, Yang et al., 2022). These resources support a broad line of regression and ranking models, including NIMA, A-Lamp, theme-aware predictors, and more recent vision-language scorers such as Q-Align and UniQA (Talebi and Milanfar, 2018, Ma et al., 2017, He et al., 2022, Wu et al., 2023, Zhou et al., 2024a). Still, the dominant setup remains pointwise, mapping from one image to a score, with preference order inferred only indirectly from independent estimates.

More recently, MLLM-based efforts have moved toward richer aesthetic reasoning. AesBench evaluates aesthetic perception in frontier MLLMs; AesExpert and UNIAA build instruction-tuned systems for critique and assessment; and ArtiMuse and the photography-focused The Photographer’s Eye move closer to expert-style analysis (Huang et al., 2024b, Huang et al., 2024a, Zhou et al., 2024b, Cao et al., 2025, Qi et al., 2025). Nevertheless, existing resources remain largely single-image, score-centric, or domain-specific. In contrast, VAB is explicitly set-based: each example is a group with matched subject matter, and the task is to identify the strongest and weakest images under controlled content. This formulation targets relative aesthetic discrimination directly, derives labels from expert consensus rather than crowd averages, and spans fine art, photography, and illustration within a unified benchmark.

B.3 Data Construction Details
Fine Art.

We commissioned 426 painting sets comprising 1,142 images across nine fine-art topics: calligraphy, Chinese painting, ink and wash, landscape color, portrait color, portrait sketch, quick sketch, still-life color, and still-life sketch. For each topic, artists received constrained prompts that fixed the subject and high-level compositional requirements while allowing variation in execution. The resulting sets preserve semantic intent while differing in composition, value structure, color harmony, and paint handling. All works were commissioned specifically for VAB rather than drawn from existing collections, which reduces the risk of contamination from publicly indexed art. Before annotation, we remove near-duplicates and discard sets with semantic mismatches or trivial cues.
Photography.

We constructed 670 photography sets comprising 1,809 images across nine topics: architecture, food and product, landscape, macro, night and astrophotography, portrait, sports, street and city, and wildlife. Each set originates from a single source photograph, many provided directly by professional photographers. We transform these source images into controlled comparison sets through two pipelines.

In the expert-edit pipeline, photographers and retouchers improve each source image using tools such as Adobe Photoshop and Lightroom (Adobe, 2026b, Adobe, 2026a), applying recomposition, color and tone correction, and content-aware expansion. The original photograph and its improved variant form a pair. For a subset of source images, multiple experts independently edit the same photograph, yielding larger candidate sets with matched subject matter and varying aesthetic quality.

In the agent-edit pipeline, each source image is first sent to a critic model, ArtiMuse (Cao et al., 2025), which produces a detailed aesthetic review. The review and the original image are then passed to a general-purpose MLLM, GPT-5 (OpenAI, 2025e), to generate two editing prompts: one for improvement and one for degradation. These prompts, together with the original image, are fed to an image-to-image model, Gemini-3-Pro-Image (Nano Banana Pro) (Google DeepMind, 2025b), to generate an improved and a degraded variant. The original, improved, and degraded images form a three-image candidate set. The exact prompt sequence is recorded in Appendix H.1.
All photography sets from both pipelines are deduplicated and reviewed for semantic consistency before annotation.
Illustration.

We constructed 271 illustration sets comprising 908 images across six topics: anime and manga, comic, concept art, digital and AI art, pixel art, and stylized 3D. The sets are derived from two distinct sources, prompt-based generation and 3D asset rendering.

In the generative pipeline, each set originates from a structured prompt that specifies subject identity, scene context, composition, camera viewpoint, lighting, and stylistic attributes. For each set, the prompt is instantiated using a single text-to-image model, such as Midjourney v7 (Midjourney, 2026), Pixellab.ai (Create M-XL) (PixelLab, 2026), or LlamaGen (Sun et al., 2024), to generate candidate images with matched subject matter and varying aesthetic quality. The prompt templates are provided in Appendix H.2.

In the 3D-rendering pipeline, each set is constructed from CC0-licensed assets sourced from Sketchfab (Creative Commons, 2009, Sketchfab, 2026). For each asset, we render multiple images by varying camera viewpoint while keeping object identity, scene semantics, lighting, and background conditions fixed. The resulting renders form candidate sets with matched subject matter and controlled variation in composition and visual presentation.
All illustration sets from both pipelines are deduplicated and reviewed for semantic consistency before annotation.

Appendix F Human Study Details
F.1 Detailed Setup and Metric Definitions
This subsection provides the full metric definitions summarized in Section 2.

Eight expert annotators evaluate identical images under both protocols. Under scoring, each annotator independently assigns an absolute score ⟦SLOT_110⟧ to each image. Under ranking, annotators provide a complete within-task ordering when presented with groups of size ⟦SLOT_111⟧. We operationalize “more scientifically sound” along three dimensions: fidelity to human comparative preference, reproducibility across annotators, and sharpness of the resulting label signal.

The study comprises 119 homogeneous-content tasks drawn directly from the curated benchmark, where all candidates share the same underlying content, and 107 heterogeneous-content tasks formed by regrouping 370 images from distinct homogeneous task groups while preserving topic consistency. Each image appears in at most one regrouped task. Examples of both settings are given in Appendix F.3.
Fidelity.

We ask whether the ranking induced by absolute scores matches the direct ranking produced by the same annotator. Let ⟦SLOT_112⟧ and ⟦SLOT_113⟧ denote annotator ⟦SLOT_114⟧’s direct rankings for homogeneous-content and heterogeneous-content tasks, and let ⟦SLOT_115⟧ denote the ranking induced by the absolute scores. We report Kendall’s ⟦SLOT_116⟧ (Kendall, 1938),
τ = C − D ( n 2 ) , \tau=\frac{C-D}{\binom{n}{2}},

where ⟦SLOT_117⟧ and ⟦SLOT_118⟧ are the numbers of concordant and discordant pairs. We compute ⟦SLOT_119⟧ for each annotator within each task, average across annotators to obtain a task-level value, and report the mean and standard deviation across tasks. We additionally report a top-1 self-consistency (SC) rate: the fraction of annotator–task pairs for which ⟦SLOT_120⟧ and the direct ranking select the same top image.
Reproducibility.

We define task-level accuracy ⟦SLOT_121⟧ as the fraction of tasks on which at least five of the eight annotators agree on the relevant label, and report ⟦SLOT_122⟧, ⟦SLOT_123⟧, and ⟦SLOT_124⟧ for both protocols.
Distinguishability.

Restricting to the 119 homogeneous-content tasks, where entropy reflects concentration of aesthetic preference rather than content mismatch, we measure the entropy of the eight annotators’ top-1 selections (Shannon, 1948),
H = − ∑ i p i log 2 p i , H=-\sum_{i}p_{i}\log_{2}p_{i},

where ⟦SLOT_125⟧ is the fraction of annotators selecting image ⟦SLOT_126⟧ as the top image in a task. Because the maximum entropy depends on task size ⟦SLOT_127⟧, we report the unnormalized quantity so that lower values directly indicate stronger concentration of top-choice judgments.

F.2 Extended Interpretation
Philosophical lens.

Our results echo the long-standing debate between Aesthetic Absolutism, which posits a context-free, intrinsic standard of beauty, and Aesthetic Relativism, which holds that judgments arise from comparison and context. Modern philosophical aesthetics has largely moved toward the relational view: people can reliably tell which image they prefer when alternatives are juxtaposed.
Statistical lens.

Scoring introduces an additional measurement layer. Annotators must first form an internal judgment and then translate it onto a numeric scale, after which pairwise preference is inferred from score differences. This pipeline adds calibration variance, scale-use heterogeneity, and extra measurement noise. Ranking measures the relative decision of interest more directly, which helps explain its higher consistency and sharper signal.
Cognitive lens.

Comparative judgment is a natural human operation. People can often say which of two images feels better before they can specify by how much. Absolute scoring is cognitively heavier because it requires maintaining an internal reference scale, calibrating intervals, and converting a qualitative impression into a number. That added abstraction likely makes scoring less stable than direct comparison.

H.4 Reward-Model Scoring Interfaces

This subsection records the model-specific scoring interfaces used to evaluate reward models on VAB. Unlike MLLMs, reward models do not share a single comparative prompt. Instead, each model scores images independently following its released evaluation method, and we convert the resulting per-image scores into within-task rankings. Across all reward models, each image is scored num_trials times, the scores are averaged, and the averaged scores are used to determine the predicted best and worst images. We use the following terminology: explicit prompt denotes prompt text exposed at the call site, implicit prompt denotes prompt text embedded inside the model library, and no prompt denotes a pure vision scorer with no language instruction.

ArtiMuse uses an implicit prompt: the instruction is hardcoded inside the released library rather than passed from our evaluation script.
At runtime, the library automatically prepends an image token before the instruction. The model outputs a two-letter code, which is then decoded back to a numerical score in ⟦SLOT_156⟧.

The scorer reads the last-token logits over the five words excellent, good, fair, poor, and bad, applies a softmax, and computes a weighted sum with weights ⟦SLOT_157⟧.

The instruction is wrapped in the mplug_owl2 conversation format with a prepended DEFAULT_IMAGE_TOKEN. The default score is the logit difference between good and poor.
